cards.front: Can traffic laws change, and whose job is it to stay informed?
cards.back: Traffic laws can change, the current rules of the road can be found by searching RCW forty-six point six one online, and staying informed is your job for as long as you drive.

cards.front: Which side of the road do you drive on, and when may you use the left side?
cards.back: Drive on the right side of the road, using the left side only briefly to pass safely and legally on a two-lane road.

cards.front: On a road with several lanes your way, which lane do you use?
cards.back: On roads with several lanes going your way, keep right except to pass, use the left lane for passing slower traffic, and obey the speed limit even while passing.

cards.front: May you pass in a carpool lane or on the shoulder?
cards.back: Carpool lanes are not passing lanes, and you should not pass or drive on the shoulder unless officials or signs tell you to.

cards.front: Which lane is for passing, and which never is?
cards.back: The left lane is for passing slower traffic, but a carpool lane is never a passing lane and the shoulder is off limits unless officials or signs direct you there.

cards.front: What if you miss a turn or exit on a freeway?
cards.back: Never drive in reverse on the road even if you miss a turn or exit, because backing up on a shoulder or freeway is illegal.

cards.front: Is hitchhiking allowed on Washington freeways?
cards.back: Hitchhiking and picking up hitchhikers on Washington freeways are both illegal.

cards.front: What are traffic control devices, and who must obey them?
cards.back: Traffic control devices are the signals, signs and road markings that direct traffic, and you are responsible for spotting and obeying all of them.

cards.front: Whose directions override traffic signals?
cards.back: Police, construction and maintenance workers and school crossing guards may direct traffic in special situations, and their directions override the signals and must be obeyed.

cards.front: How do you treat an intersection whose signal is not working?
cards.back: At a traffic signal that is not working, treat the intersection as a four-way stop: stop completely, yield to traffic on your right, and go carefully when safe.

cards.front: Can you drive straight through a dark traffic signal?
cards.back: A dark or broken traffic signal is handled as a four-way stop with a full stop and yielding to the right, not as a signal you may drive through.

cards.front: What do you do at a solid red light, and when may you turn right?
cards.back: At a solid red light, stop and wait for green and a clear intersection, though after a full stop you may turn right if no sign forbids a turn on red and there is room to enter traffic.

cards.front: When may you turn left on a red light?
cards.back: After a complete stop at a red light, you may also turn left onto a one-way street when no sign prohibits it and there is room to merge.

cards.front: What do a flashing red light and a red arrow mean?
cards.back: A flashing red light works exactly like a stop sign, while a red arrow means you may not go in the arrow's direction.

cards.front: How do solid red, flashing red and a red arrow differ?
cards.back: A solid red means stop and wait for green, a flashing red means stop and then go in turn like a stop sign, and a red arrow forbids only the arrow's direction.

cards.front: What does a solid yellow light mean, and what if you are already in the intersection?
cards.back: A solid yellow light warns that red is coming, so slow and prepare to stop, but if you are already in the intersection keep going at the posted speed, never speeding up to beat it.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow light mean?
cards.back: A flashing yellow light means the same as a yield sign, so treat the intersection as uncontrolled and go only when you have the right-of-way.

cards.front: How does a solid yellow differ from a flashing yellow?
cards.back: A solid yellow tells you to prepare to stop because red is next, whereas a flashing yellow tells you to yield and proceed when it is your right-of-way.

cards.front: Caught in the intersection on a yellow, should you speed up?
cards.back: Being caught in the intersection on a yellow means continue at the posted speed, not accelerate past it to clear the light.

cards.front: What does a yellow arrow warn you about?
cards.back: A yellow arrow warns that the arrow will soon turn red, so get ready to stop and yield to oncoming traffic.

cards.front: What does a solid green light mean?
cards.back: A solid green light means go once the intersection is clear, still yielding to pedestrians and to emergency vehicles as the law requires.

cards.front: Who has the right-of-way when you turn left on a solid green?
cards.back: Turning left on a solid green, oncoming traffic has the right-of-way, so wait where you can see approaching cars and turn when there is a gap.

cards.front: What does a green arrow give you?
cards.back: A green arrow gives you the right-of-way in its direction, with no oncoming, crossing or pedestrian traffic expected while it shows.

cards.front: How does a left turn on a solid green differ from one on a green arrow?
cards.back: A solid green lets you turn left only after yielding to oncoming traffic, while a green arrow gives you the right-of-way for that turn.

cards.front: Does Washington use flashing green lights?
cards.back: Washington does not use flashing green lights, though British Columbia uses them to warn that pedestrians are waiting to cross.

cards.front: How does a freeway ramp meter work?
cards.back: A freeway ramp meter works like a normal signal: on red stop at the white stop line, and on green continue up the ramp.

cards.front: What does each sign color mean?
cards.back: Sign colors carry meaning: red for prohibited or restricted actions, orange for construction warnings, yellow for general warnings, white for regulations, green for guidance, blue for motorist services and brown for recreation and culture.

cards.front: What do fluorescent yellow-green signs warn about?
cards.back: Fluorescent yellow-green signs warn of school, pedestrian and bicycle activity.

cards.front: How do orange, plain yellow and yellow-green warning signs differ?
cards.back: Orange warns of construction and maintenance, plain yellow warns of general road conditions, and fluorescent yellow-green warns of school, pedestrian and bicycle activity.

cards.front: What do white, green, blue and brown signs mark?
cards.back: White marks a regulatory sign, green gives directions, blue points to motorist services and brown marks recreation or cultural areas.

cards.front: What must you do at a stop sign and at a yield sign?
cards.back: At a stop sign, stop at the line, crosswalk or corner, check all directions for vehicles and pedestrians, and yield the right-of-way, while a yield sign means slow down and let traffic with the right-of-way go first.

cards.front: How does a stop sign differ from a yield sign?
cards.back: A stop sign always requires a full stop, whereas a yield sign requires slowing down and letting traffic that has the right-of-way cross first.

cards.front: Can you be ticketed below the posted maximum speed?
cards.back: A posted maximum speed applies to ideal conditions, so you can be ticketed for going too fast for slippery or foggy conditions even below the limit.

cards.front: What does a minimum speed limit require?
cards.back: Some roads post a minimum speed limit, and you must drive at least that fast so you do not endanger other drivers.

cards.front: How do maximum and minimum speed limits differ?
cards.back: A maximum speed limit is a ceiling for ideal conditions, while a minimum speed limit is a floor you must reach so you are not a hazard.

cards.front: What do automated traffic safety cameras record, and who gets the ticket?
cards.back: Automated traffic safety cameras record drivers who fail to stop for a steady red light or a railroad crossing signal or who speed in a school zone, their locations are clearly marked, and tickets are mailed to the vehicle owner.

cards.front: What do speed warning signs and variable speed limit signs do?
cards.back: Speed warning signs recommend a slower speed for a hazard such as a curve, and digital variable speed limit signs change posted limits and can close lanes ahead of slow traffic.

cards.front: What does a red circle with a red slash over a symbol mean?
cards.back: A red circle with a red slash over a symbol forbids that action, such as a left turn, right turn or U-turn.

cards.front: What do Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs look like and mean?
cards.back: A Do Not Enter sign is square with a white horizontal bar inside a circle, and a Wrong Way sign means you are headed against traffic and must stop and turn around at once.

cards.front: How do Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs differ?
cards.back: Do Not Enter warns you before you turn into a street from the wrong direction, while Wrong Way tells you that you are already traveling against traffic and must turn around.

cards.front: What is a shared center left-turn lane for?
cards.back: A shared center left-turn lane is reserved for drivers turning left from either direction and may not be used for through travel or passing.

cards.front: What must you do in a highway work zone, and what happens to fines?
cards.back: In a highway work zone everyone must yield to workers, equipment and vehicles with flashing yellow lights, and fines double for offenses there when workers are present.

cards.front: What do service signs point to?
cards.back: Service signs point to services such as hospitals, electric vehicle charging stations and rest areas.

cards.front: What do destination signs and route number signs tell you?
cards.back: Destination signs give directions and distances to places such as cities and airports, and the shape and color of a route number sign tell you whether it is an interstate, U.S., state, city or county road.

cards.front: Which signs are drivers responsible for knowing?
cards.back: The guide shows only some Washington signs, yet drivers are responsible for knowing every sign, including city and county ones.

cards.front: What does an added lane sign mark?
cards.back: An added lane sign marks a lane that joins from the right where no merging is required.

recap_hooks.text: Laws change, so stay informed; drive on the right and keep right except to pass.
Carpool lanes and shoulders are not for passing, never reverse on the road, and no hitchhiking on freeways.
Obey every traffic control device, and people directing traffic override the signals.
A dark signal is a four-way stop; solid red means wait, flashing red is a stop sign, a red arrow forbids that way.
After a full stop you may turn right on red, or left onto a one-way street, when allowed.
Solid yellow means prepare to stop, but keep going if already in the intersection without speeding up.
Flashing yellow means yield, and a yellow arrow is about to turn red.
Green means go once clear; on a solid green left turn, oncoming traffic goes first, but a green arrow gives you the turn.
Washington has no flashing green, and ramp meters work like normal signals.
Each sign color has a meaning, and yellow-green warns of school, pedestrian and bicycle activity.
Stop fully at a stop sign; at a yield sign, slow and let others go first.
The maximum is for ideal conditions and the minimum is a floor.
Cameras mail tickets to owners, and warning and variable signs adjust speed for conditions.
A red slash forbids an action, Do Not Enter warns before you turn in, and Wrong Way means turn around now.
Center turn lanes are for left turns, work zones double fines, and you must know every sign.
